voiceName: Hey Its Brad - Clear Narrator for Documentary

prompts.beat-01: [warmly] Imagine a neighbor asks where they can get help using a computer. You may already have a familiar library, community center, or veterans' organization in mind. Use that experience as a starting point, then verify what is available now. [short pause] [interested] Today's search tools answer in full sentences, so our first skill is asking well, and our second is checking what the answer says. Our task is to find a suitable public service, record enough evidence to revisit it, and organize a fictional handout without exposing private information. You can use a different local service that matters to you. The names and details in this demonstration are examples, not a claim about any particular organization. A useful search ends with a supported decision, not just an answer that sounds confident.
prompts.beat-02: [interested] Search tools now answer in sentences. [short pause] Google may show an AI Overview above the results, and AI Mode lets you keep asking follow-up questions. Both work best when you ask the way you would ask a librarian. [short pause] Say what you need, where you are, and what matters to you. Where can I get free computer help near Beckley, West Virginia, in the evening? is far more useful than computer help. If the first answer is too broad, ask a follow-up, such as which of these are open on Saturdays. [short pause] [encouraging] Pause and write a question for your chosen community task. Include the service, the place, and one detail that matters to you. Then ask one follow-up.
prompts.beat-03: [reassuring] An AI answer is a quick summary written from many pages. It can sound sure and still be wrong, out of date, or about a different town. So treat it as a lead, not a source. [short pause] Look for the links beside or beneath it, and open the organization's own page. Ask who published it, when it was updated, and whether it answers your question. If the summary and the page disagree, trust the responsible organization, and confirm hours by phone before you travel. [short pause] Never type private details into a question, such as a Social Security number, a bank number, or medical information. [short pause] [encouraging] Pause, open one source from your answer, and find one detail it confirms and one it does not.
prompts.beat-04: [warmly] Suppose you find a useful service today and need it again next month. [curious] A note saying good website will not be enough. Record the organization, the page title, the web address, the date you checked it, and the particular fact you plan to use. [short pause] If an AI answer led you to the page, record the page it pointed to, not the summary. A bookmark helps you return, but it does not freeze the page or prove that the information remains current. In your handout, distinguish a checked fact from your own interpretation. If the page does not answer a question, write needs confirmation rather than filling the gap with a guess. [warmly] This is the digital equivalent of writing the source beside a number in a household notebook.
